title: Patron saints
hookLine: Catholics ask particular saints to pray for particular needs

cards: Lost your keys? Some Catholics will tell you, half laughing and fully serious, to ask Saint Anthony. A small statue of Saint Joseph on a carpenter's workbench.
A medal of Saint Christopher clipped to a car's sun visor. A doctor with a picture of Saint Luke in her locker. It can look like a phone directory of heaven: one saint per department.

teach.h: A SAINT FOR A PLACE, A PEOPLE, A WORK.
teach.b: A patron saint is a saint Catholics ask to pray for a particular place, people, work or need. Countries have patrons, and cities, and parishes. So do jobs.
Joseph, the carpenter, for workers. Luke, called a physician in a letter of Paul, for doctors. Cecilia, remembered for music, for musicians.

Thomas More, the lawyer who refused to swear an oath against his conscience, for politicians. Sometimes a pope names a patron officially; sometimes the connection grew up among ordinary people over time.
Underneath every patron is a simple idea from the letter of James, in the Douay-Rheims: "pray one for another, that you may be saved. For the continual prayer of a just man availeth much."
Catholics believe the saints are alive with God, and so they can still do what friends do: pray for you. The Catechism says the saints don't stop interceding for us.
A patron is not a replacement for God, and not a vending machine for favors. In Catholic teaching, asking a saint for help means asking that saint to pray with you, to God. Why a particular saint?

teach.h: A FRIEND WHO KNOWS THE JOB.
teach.b: A saint who worked with wood knows splinters.

teach.h: THE CONTINUAL PRAYER OF A JUST MAN AVAILETH MUCH.
teach.b: A saint who was a doctor knows the night shift. Asking a patron is a little like asking a colleague who has done your work before, and done it with love, to put in a word.

how: Catholics ask patron saints to pray for them in particular needs, places or kinds of work; parishes and countries keep their patron's feast, and some people keep a patron's image or medal at work or at home.

o: a saint who founded a parish or a city
a saint asked to pray for a place, work or need
a wealthy donor who pays for a church

s: in Catholic teaching, a patron saint answers prayers in place of God
Catholics ask a saint to pray with them, to God.
patrons can be named officially by a pope or grow up among ordinary people
both happen: some by decree, some by long custom.
only countries and cities have patron saints
jobs, parishes, peoples and needs have patrons too.

games.q: the letter of James gives a reason for asking others to pray for you. what does it say?
o: the continual prayer of a just man availeth much.
games.why: James tells Christians to pray one for another. Catholics extend that to the saints, who they believe are alive with God.

practice: Your work might be a job, school, raising children, caring for someone, or looking for work: bring it to mind, its hardest part, the hour of the day it weighs most.
If you pray, ask a saint you already know to pray for you in that hard part; if you don't, hold your work kindly, as something worth doing well.

wordCard.voice: Patron. A saint Catholics ask to pray for a particular place, people, work or need: a friend in heaven who knows the job.

orig.note: Latin: protector, advocate, someone who stands up for you; the word behind patron saint.

carryVoice: Your line: a friend for the job. Not a department of heaven. That's day nine hundred fifty-one.
